title: Banks are choosing how much AI to let in
dek: A card block, a regulator's report and a Thai growth warning show three ways finance is deciding how far to go.

body.head: One bank draws a line
body.text: Start with the most concrete decision of the weekend. The Wall Street Journal reported that JPMorgan Chase is blocking AI agents from shopping with its customers' credit cards when customers give the agent their card number, while cards from Bank of America, Capital One and Citigroup are already being used by agents when customers allow it, the Journal said.
support: JPMorgan Chase is blocking artificial intelligence (AI) agents from shopping with its customers’ credit cards when customers give the agent their card number, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday (Nov. 13).
Cards from Bank of America , Capital One and Citigroup are already being used by agents when customers allow it, the Journal said.

body.head: The workaround has a price
body.text: Stripe gets around the block, because its Link wallet gives the agent a one-time virtual card. Merchants have complained to Visa and Mastercard that this virtual card costs more on average to accept, since it is classified as a commercial card rather than a consumer card, the Journal reported, and for those of us in payments that is the detail to watch.
support: Stripe gets around the block. Its Link wallet gives the agent a one-time virtual card instead of the customer’s own card.

Merchants have complained to Visa and Mastercard that the virtual card costs more on average to accept than the shopper’s own card because it is classified as a commercial card rather than a consumer card, the Journal reported.

body.head: A regulator sees an opportunity
body.text: Meanwhile the OCC, the US federal banking regulator, said in its latest risk report that banks of all sizes are continuing to explore ways to leverage Super Intelligence. The OCC said credit risk in the loan portfolios of OCC-supervised banks remains modest overall, and that the technology creates opportunities to enhance efficiency and internal controls.
support: Banks of all sizes are continuing to explore ways to leverage Super Intelligence (SI).
Credit risk in the loan portfolios of OCC-supervised banks remains modest overall.
The growing availability and advancement of SI create opportunities to enhance efficiency and internal controls as well as to improve analytics and customize services.

body.head: Thailand watches the other side
body.text: At the same time ttb analytics in Thailand pointed to the other side of the boom. It said growth is heavily concentrated in AI-linked electronics, and that if the global AI boom experiences a bubble burst, the impact on Thailand will be immediate and pronounced, especially within financial markets.
support: Growth is heavily concentrated in AI-linked electronics.

If the global AI boom experiences a bubble burst, the impact on Thailand will be immediate and pronounced—especially within financial markets—because we are formally indexed as a key upstream and downstream supplier.

body.head: What to ask your own team
body.text: Put side by side, these stories show finance deciding in real time how much AI to let in, and each of us can ask where our own organization stands: do we let agents use customers' cards, and what would it cost us if the AI boom turned?

suggestion: A line on how your own clients ask about agents paying with their cards would fit at the end of the last section.
